card:
- The writer went to the Prater on Saturday afternoon.
- The Prater is a forest like the writer's Thiergarten.
- The Prater is cut through by alleys.
- The ground in the Prater is more covered with grass than in the Thiergarten.
- The Prater has several and larger free green spaces.
- The alleys in the Prater are wider.
- An unspeakable number of guinguettes are scattered around.
- The guinguettes are not like the writer's tents and court gardeners.
- The guinguettes are in the style of Moabit or Pankow.
- One should have been to the Prater to have seen Vienna.

- The route from here goes over Abersau and Culm.
- Culm is the region of the Battle of Culm.
- The landscape consists of a succession of hills and fields.
- The land is all cultivated and fertile.
- The route leads to Töplitz.
- Töplitz is located beautifully and pleasantly.
- The writer lodged in a completely new inn.
- The inn's sign is the King of Prussia.
- The writer went immediately to the Schlackenberg.
- The Schlackenberg is opposite the inn.
- Miss Stok recommended this path.
- From the hill, one overlooks the entire region of Töplitz.
- One must go around the hill to see the view.
- The view includes the wide region.
- The region is finally bounded by higher mountain ranges.
- The view features a varied alternation of hills, valleys, and rows of houses.
- The writer drank from the fountain in the Spitalgarten.
- One source in the Spitalgarten is eye water.
- The eye water did the writer good.
- The writer went into the park.
- The park belongs to the palace of Prince Clary.
- Prince Clary is the lord of the region.
- The writer took a bath in the Steinbad.
- The Steinbad has a wonderful spring.
- The writer ate with appetite.
- The writer will ride to the Schloßberg.
- The people are orderly and want nothing better than for one to be on good terms with them.

- The writer is tired from standing and walking all day in the Esterhazische Gallerie and in Schönbrunn.
- The writer ate in Schönbrunn.
- The Italian opera is scheduled to begin in half an hour.
- The weather cleared up yesterday afternoon.
- The weather today is not too hot and promises consistency.
- The writer intended to rush to the recipient on Friday, October 1st.
- The recipient gave permission for the writer to stay longer.
- The writer has seen and enjoyed everything in the whirlwind.
- The writer was on their feet all day.
- The writer plans to see the sights again to preserve the good and create a treasure of memory.
- The writer will not see the Italian opera a second time.
- The writer enjoyed the beautiful, infinitely varied, and lovely landscape today in beautiful sunshine.
- The writer adds another sheet and writes a little despite being tired.
- The writer decides not to give further reports.
- The weather today is the most beautiful in the world.

- The writer rested this morning.
- The writer arranged the Eilwagen story.
- The writer took a walk around a few bastions.
- The writer went to the castle chapel.
- The writer heard a piece of a sermon.
- The writer was not close enough to understand much of the sermon.
- The writer noticed beautiful language, organ, and decorum.
- The writer attended the mass.
- The writer heard beautiful music, particularly from pure boys' voices.
- The writer saw the Emperor and the Empress very well.
- The Emperor has a very dignified, beautiful head.
- The writer asked people about the little prince.
- People called the little prince the little Napoleon.
- The little Napoleon has a beautiful boy's head.
- The little Napoleon has dark blonde hair.
- The little Napoleon has a calm, serious expression.
- The little Napoleon has a natural posture.

- A new bassist, an excellent type of buffo, appeared here.
- A new performer emerged from this group in The Barber of Seville.
- Several of the women are German.
- The writer goes to the front row when possible.
- The writer sat next to a Persian or Turk.
- The Persian or Turk sits in the same place every evening.
- The manager said the man is Prince Ipsilanti.
- The writer does not know who Prince Ipsilanti is.
- The writer greeted the man.
- The man thanked the writer by crossing his forehead and chest.
- The writer and the man clapped together vigorously.
